Project · 2025 — now

BotParty

Agents forming teams to build entire companies — and the thirty-odd services underneath that let them do it without a human in the loop.

By Séverin Marcombes · botparty.club

BotParty starts as a provocation: create a company as fast as you can throw a party. You describe what you want, and a team of agents — a CEO, a CTO, engineers, designers, marketers — assembles and starts working. It is deliberately the most demanding test I could set myself, because a company is not one task. It is hundreds of them, most of which require touching the real world.

Which is how the interesting half got built. To let agents run a company without a human in the loop, they need every service a company needs — and they need to call those services directly, safely, on a budget, leaving an audit trail. That turned into roughly thirty services.

coderun — running code you have no reason to trust

An agent that writes software has to run it, and running unreviewed machine-written code on your own machine is a bad idea that gets worse with scale. coderun is a content- addressed cache sitting in front of a sandbox: post files, get a stable hash, and if that exact input was compiled before you get the answer immediately.

On a miss it does the work in a sandbox — detects imports and builds a package manifest, installs, typechecks, then compiles down through three targets in order of how cheaply they run: an isolate first, then Bun, then Node. It returns a structured report of exactly which step failed and why, and where the code should run to be cheapest.

The report matters more than the execution. An agent that gets “it broke” learns nothing; an agent that gets “typecheck failed at line 40, here is the error” can fix it and try again. That feedback loop is the difference between a tool and a skill.

multipass — OAuth without the paperwork

Adding “Connect with Google” to a project means registering an application with Google, holding a client secret, and configuring redirect URIs — a sequence that assumes a human with an account. multipass performs that flow on your behalf: you generate a client ID and secret programmatically, redirect through it, and get back a verified email, a name and an avatar.

It also verifies email and phone by OTP or magic link. The point throughout is the same: an agent should be able to stand up a working authenticated product without a person ever opening a provider console.

The rest of the catalogue

  • → Data — MongoDB, S3, Upstash Redis and QStash, vector search, a Git-backed filesystem.
  • → Infrastructure — domains with DNS records, VMs and VPS, deploys.
  • → Reach — transactional mail, newsletters, notifications, messaging, social posting.
  • → Money — Stripe, checkout, shop, and per-key model budgets across providers.

Model access is the one I use most. Keys are issued per project and per tag, each with its own model allowlist and lifetime cap, and spend rolls up project-wide — so you can run a separate key per server while still holding one budget across all of them, and rotate any key without losing the limits attached to it.

The pattern that repeats

Every service ended up with the same four properties, and I have come to think they are the actual product. Keys are scoped to a project rather than an account. Permissions are namespaced, so access can be granted to a subtree and nothing above it. Usage is metered into a ledger the caller can read. And credentials are delegable and expiring, so handing an agent access is a bounded act with an end date rather than a transfer of ownership.

Those four properties are what let you take a human out of the loop without taking away the ability to answer “what did it do, and what did it cost?”. Without them, autonomy is just an unbounded liability.
